prompt: What does listing debug.log in .gitignore do?
hint: It is about what Git sees.

choices.text: Deletes debug.log from the disk
choices.why: The file stays exactly where it is.

choices.text: It drops out of status and add .
choices.why: Right. Git stops showing it and git add . skips it. That is all ignoring does.

choices.text: Encrypts it so nobody else can read it
choices.why: Git encrypts nothing.

choices.text: Removes it from every earlier commit
choices.why: Nothing in the history changes.

choices.text: No, it is a personal file
choices.why: That is the global ignore file. The project's list is shared.

choices.text: No, Git reads it from the server
choices.why: Git reads it from the working tree, so it has to be in every clone.

choices.text: Yes, so every clone ignores the same files
choices.why: Right. Nobody commits node_modules/ by accident.

choices.text: Only if the project has a node_modules/ folder
choices.why: Every project with ignore rules benefits from sharing them.

prompt: To find which rule ignores debug.log: git ___ -v debug.log
hint: Two words joined by a hyphen.

prompt: Match each .gitignore line to what it ignores.
hint: One description is not what any of these lines does.

pairs.right: Every file ending in .log, in any folder
That folder and everything inside it
The build folder at the top of the project only
An exception: keep.log is not ignored

prompt: settings.local was committed, then added to .gitignore. Ana edits it. What does git status show?
hint: Ignoring applies to files Git is not tracking yet.

choices.text: Nothing; the file is ignored
choices.why: It is tracked, so the rule does not apply to it.

choices.text: M settings.local
choices.why: Right. A tracked file's edits show like any other.

choices.text: An error about the conflicting rule
choices.why: There is no conflict to report; tracking simply wins.

choices.text: ?? settings.local
choices.why: ?? is untracked, and this file is tracked.

prompt: What does git rm --cached settings.local do?
hint: --cached means the staging area, not the disk.

choices.text: Deletes the file from the disk and the history
choices.why: The disk keeps it, and earlier commits keep theirs.

choices.text: Stops tracking it and leaves it on the disk
choices.why: Right. The next commit records its removal from the project.

choices.text: Clears Git's cache of the file
choices.why: Cached here is an old name for the staging area.

choices.text: Adds the file to .gitignore for you
choices.why: It touches no .gitignore.

prompt: A payment key was committed and pushed an hour ago, then deleted in a new commit. What is the first thing to do?

choices.text: Nothing more; the new commit removed it
choices.why: git show HEAD~1:.env still prints it.

choices.text: Revoke the key and make a new one
choices.why: Right. It is the only step that fixes anything; the rest is cleaning up.

choices.text: Rewrite the history with git filter-repo
choices.why: That may follow, but copies already exist; the key must change first.

choices.text: Add .env to .gitignore
choices.why: That prevents the next accident and does nothing about this one.

prompt: After the key was committed, pushed and then deleted in a later commit, where can it still be found? Choose all that apply.
hint: Deleting a file does not change old commits.

choices.text: In the commit that added it
choices.why: Yes. git show prints it.

choices.text: In every clone made since the push
choices.why: Yes. Every clone has every commit.

choices.text: On the shared copy
choices.why: Yes. It was pushed there.

choices.text: In the working tree of whoever deleted it
choices.why: The file is gone from the tree of the commit; this capture kept it on disk, ignored, but that is not where the danger is.

prompt: A 1 MB photo is committed three times with small edits. Roughly how much does the repository grow?
hint: Images do not compress, and every version is kept.

choices.text: About 1 MB: only the last version counts
choices.why: Every version stays in the history.

choices.text: Almost nothing, since Git stores differences
choices.why: Lesson 1: Git stores snapshots, and a new image is a whole new file.

choices.text: About 3 MB
choices.why: Right. The capture grew by about three megabytes.

choices.text: It depends on how many branches there are
choices.why: Branches are names; they cost nothing.

prompt: With Git LFS tracking *.jpg, what does git show HEAD:front.jpg print?
hint: What went into the history instead of the photo?

choices.text: The photo's bytes
choices.why: The history holds a pointer; the bytes are in LFS storage.

choices.text: An error, since LFS files cannot be shown
choices.why: It shows exactly what is stored: the pointer.

choices.text: A three-line pointer: version, hash and size
choices.why: Right. That is what the commit actually contains.

choices.text: The photo, downloaded from the server
choices.why: git show reads the history, which holds the pointer.

prompt: git lfs track "*.jpg" writes its rule into a file called ___, which is committed with the project.
Which of these is the best candidate for Git LFS?

choices.text: A 40 MB design file edited every week
choices.why: Right. Large, and each version would stay in every clone.

choices.text: A 4 KB logo that never changes
choices.why: Small and fixed costs nothing in plain Git.

choices.text: The site's index.html
choices.why: Text compresses well and diffs well; plain Git is right for it.

choices.text: A password file
choices.why: Secrets belong in no history, LFS included.

prompt: What does the site's commit record about the styles submodule?

choices.text: A copy of every file in styles/
choices.why: The files belong to the submodule's own repository.

choices.text: One id: the exact version pinned
choices.why: Right. d874c59, until somebody moves it on purpose.

choices.text: The branch to follow, always its newest commit
choices.why: Following a branch automatically is exactly what pinning avoids.

choices.text: Only the address, fetched fresh each time
choices.why: The address is in .gitmodules; the commit pins the version.

prompt: Bruno clones the site and finds styles/ empty. Why, and what fixes it?
hint: A plain clone does not fetch submodules.

choices.text: The submodule was never committed; commit it again
choices.why: It was committed: .gitmodules and the pinned commit are there.

choices.text: Submodules need update --init
choices.why: Right. A plain clone skips them; git submodule update --init fetches styles/. Or clone with --recurse-submodules next time.

choices.text: styles/ is ignored by .gitignore
choices.why: Ignoring has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Bruno needs Git LFS installed
choices.why: LFS is for large files, not submodules.

prompt: Match each problem to the tool this lesson gives for it.
hint: One tool on the right fixes none of them.

pairs.left: A tracked file that should stop being tracked
Another project pinned to an exact commit

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them imagine that deleting or ignoring changes the past.

choices.text: Adding a committed file to .gitignore stops Git tracking it
choices.why: It needs git rm --cached as well.

choices.text: Deleting a secret in a new commit removes it from the history
choices.why: The commit that added it still has it.

choices.text: Git LFS needs to be installed by everybody on the team
choices.why: Yes, or they get pointers instead of files.

choices.text: A submodule is pinned to a commit, not a branch
choices.why: Yes. It moves only when somebody commits the move.

choices.text: The global ignore file is for patterns about your machine
choices.why: Yes, like .DS_Store.
